1. **Did they actually see it?**  
   Ask who saw it. If it’s just a neighbor’s dog acting weird, maybe. But if it’s my phone, I check it twice. Real-time, not after.

2. **How many times did it happen?**  
   One time, maybe. Two? Maybe. Ten? That’s a pattern. I need to know if it’s a fluke or actually happening a lot.

3. **Where? Where were they?**  
   Is it just my backyard or the whole block? Same thing over here, same thing over there? If it’s everywhere, maybe it’s not a fluke.

4. **Who else saw it?**  
   If I’m the only one, maybe I’m looking for it. If three people from different sides of the street all say the same thing, that’s worth checking.

5. **What did I see? What did I hear?**  
   I need the details. If they just say “the lights went weird,” but I can’t check, I can’t believe it. But if they show me the app, I can look.

6. I look for the same thing again myself.  
   If I can’t repeat it, I can’t prove it. If I can, I keep watching. That’s how you know.

7. Compare it to something else.  
   If everyone else is fine and mine’s off, maybe it’s just a glitch. If everyone’s off, maybe it’s the whole system.

8. I don’t care if someone’s “trust me” unless I can see it.  
   Even then, I want to see it twice. Once is a guess. Twice is maybe. Three times, I start to believe.

So, I wait for more. I ask who else saw it. I check the clock, the time, the phone. If it’s weird and only me, I ignore it. If it’s weird and everyone else has it too, then I start looking for a pattern. That’s when I move fast.

Bottom line: Anecdotes don’t mean much until they’re checked by someone else, and by the same rules. Then we talk.

### 2. **Did I see the red?**
I mean, the stop sign, the “no, no, no” light, the guy yelling “turn back!” I ignore it and walk forward. That’s me, not the street. I should have known.

1. **Take a breath.** First thing I do is count to three and try to calm down. Panicking makes it worse.

2. **Check what actually happened.** I go back and look at the data, the notes, the emails—see what really broke. Sometimes I was wrong, sometimes it was both of us. I don’t pretend it was just me.

3. own what I did, but don’t make it about me. I tell the team what I did wrong and how I fixed it this time. I don’t need to say it was their fault, just say “my end was messed up, here’s what I’ll do now.”

4. If they’re still taking the blame, I ask them what they need from me. Maybe they need to redo it, or maybe they just need to say yes or no. I help them fix it, not me. We both redo it right this time.

5. After, I talk to my boss. I give my real numbers, my part, and what I’m doing to make it right. If I can’t fix it, I tell them who’s on it and who’s helping. I don so the next time it doesn’t happen again.

6. If they still won’t own it, I keep my notes and my fix. Next time it happens, I’m ready. I can’t control them, but I can control my part.

When something goes wrong, I don’t rush to point fingers or blame someone right away. Instead, I take a step back and make sure everyone knows I’m listening. First, I check the facts—what actually happened, exactly when, and what the system or process said before it broke. I look at the logs, the notes, the data. I ask the same questions twice, just to be sure I got it right.

Once I have the right picture, I talk to the people who were there. I let them walk me through what they were doing, what they noticed, what they thought would be fine. Sometimes they see something I missed, and that’s useful. I don’t interrupt, I just nod and wait. I want the real story, not the last version I saw.

After I have everything, I write it down—my notes, not anyone else’s. I list what went wrong, why it happened, and what we can check next time. We look for the root, not just the mess. Then we talk about what we can do to stop it from happening again. If we can’t fix it tonight, we set a time and come back. I make sure the fix is in the next checklist, and I check it twice before we call it done. 

And after that, I tell the team. Not to brag, just so they know it won’t happen again. And I check the next shift’s run before I leave. That’s how we make it better.

steered:
Great question. When a new tool or technique looks like it could change everything but I don’t know how it’ll break, I don’t just trust the shiny numbers. Here’s how I’d look at it—step by step, because the risk isn’’t zero and neither is the upside.

First, I want to see the whole picture, not just the highlights. So I start with the demo or the chart that shows what’s different, but then I zoom in on the rest. What’s the window? How big? How fast does it move? What’s it missing? And what’s it can’t do yet? If they say “it’s 90% right, just wait till next week,” I’m not buying it.

Then I ask: what’s it touch? Which pieces? Which parts of the process, which files, which people? I need to know exactly what gets changed, and what doesn’t. If it’s only one thing, that’s easier to check. If it’s the whole stack, I need to know why.

Next, I want to see the old way and the new way side by side. I make a checklist: what’s the same, what’s different, what’s missing, what’s extra. Then I count the things I can’t control. How long till I know if it’s safe? How long till I can roll back if it goes wrong? If there’s no undo, that’s a red flag.

I always ask who’s fixing it if it blows up—me, the client, the boss? And who’s paying if it’s my mistake? And who’s got the phone number for the support line? If nobody does, that’s a no.

Then I check the logs. I want to see what happens when it’s not pretty. I want to see the errors, the gaps, the things that don’t line up. If the demo was perfect and the real data looks wrong, that’s a sign.

I always want a plan B. What if it just stops working? What if I can’t get it back? I need a patch, a backup, a way to go back to the old way. If not, we wait.

And I keep asking: how much can we lose if it’s wrong? How much can we gain if it’s right? And if we can’t measure it, we can’t trust it. So I want numbers, not promises.

If they can’t give me the real data, I can’t see if it’s working. If they can’t show me the mistakes, I can’t fix them when it goes wrong. If they can’t say what it costs to fix it, that’s the last thing I care about.

So I wait until I’ve got the truth, not the wish. Then we talk about the risk and the fix together. That’s how you keep the whole picture.

That’s a really good question—and it’s one that comes up all the time in medicine, business, policy, and even when I’m picking what to eat for dinner. There’s no universal answer, but I can give you some thinking to help you figure it out yourself.

First, let’s break it down:  
You’re waiting to act, and if I don’t move now, something might go wrong later. But if I do this now, I might mess it up and lose even more. When does the “don’t move” risk get bigger than the “do it wrong” risk?

It depends on a few things:
- How fast things are changing. If the problem’s getting worse every minute, waiting is just losing more. If it’s still the same, I can wait.
- How bad it gets if I wait. If letting it sit means someone’s going to be sick for a week, I don’t wait. If I wait, I lose a night’s sleep, I can wait.
- How bad it gets if I mess up. If I pick the wrong drug, the wrong cut, the wrong pitch, the wrong call—well, I know what happens. If I just wait, the patient might throw up on the floor and the nurse has to mop it up. If I pick the wrong medicine, the kid throws up for three hours. Which is worse?
- There’s always a cost of moving. If I change the IV wrong, I waste ten minutes. If I wait, the patient’s going to throw up in five minutes. I know what to do. I just do it.

Rule of thumb: If the thing getting worse is going to make three times as bad if I wait, and I can fix it in two minutes, I move. If I can’t fix it and the mess is already on the floor, I move. If I’m changing the wrong thing and I’ve already got the right one in the other tray, I just swap it. If I’m not sure which one’s right and I change the wrong one, I wait and count the seconds till the clock says stop.

But the best I can tell you is:  
When the thing that’s not moving stops being small. When the cost of waiting is bigger than the cost of messing up. When I can see the difference in my head, not in my head.

So you look at it, count the seconds, and make the call. That’s the only way.

This is a tricky one—when you do everything exactly right, but the numbers just don’t add up, and now we’re late. It’s not like I ever check the clock, but… okay, let’s say it happens. Here’s how I’d handle it, and why you should too.

First, I double-check my math. Maybe I missed a step. Maybe I copied the wrong number from the sheet. If it’s my math, I fix it. If it’s the client’s numbers, I ask them to send it again. No one moves fast enough for my luck.

If it’s really their numbers, I tell them. Not “your numbers are wrong,” just “hey, I got it again and it’s different. Can you send the real one?” That way, we’re both on the same page. If they can’t send it, I start guessing and flag it for the next batch. I don’t guess. I write it down what I think, but I tell them I’m waiting on the real one.

If we’re already late and I can’t change it, I look for what we can do next. Can we drop the last thing? Can we shift the order? Can we tell the customer it’s going to be late and give them a new time? I check the schedule again—maybe we can skip the last step and just call it done. Or I break it into two parts and send what we got, and send the rest tomorrow.

I never let the client think it’s their fault. I tell them what happened, what I did, and what’s left to do. If we can’t make it this week, I move the rest to next week and send it then. I keep the notes and the steps so we don’t lose it. And next time, I check the math three times.

If I can’t get it done right, I tell them. If I can’t get it done on time, I tell them first, and we fix it. That’s the only way it’s going to be right next time. And if I miss the deadline anyway, I check my notes and start over from the beginning. That’s how you get it right next time. Not because I’m perfect, but because I know what I did wrong and I do it different next time.

So, you just keep your head and your hands steady. Fix what you can, tell the truth, and we’ll get it right next time.

That’s a great question—there’s never really a right or wrong answer, but people’s choices say a lot about what they’re chasing. Here’s how I’d break it down:

If you’re offered something brand new, untouched, nothing’s worked like it before—well, that’s a big deal. You get to be the first to see if it’ll fit or not. That’s risky, but if it works, it’s all me, no one else got it right. There’s that rush, that maybe-you’ll-be-the-one kind of hope. People who go for the new thing are usually hoping to find something better, or at least different. Sometimes it’s just because the old one got boring, or the same. Sometimes it’s because they want to prove they can make it work before anyone else does.

But the old one, the one that already fits, it’s steady. You know what you’re getting, you know how it moves, how it looks, how it sounds. You don’t have to fight the machine. People who fix what’s good, tweak it, make it smoother—they know the mistakes, they know what works. They’re not gambling, they’re just making it a little better. That’s comfort. That’s control.

So, which pulls more? New or old? Depends on why. If you want to see what could be, you go for new. If you want to make what is just a little bit more, you keep working on the old. Both got their place. But if I had to pick, I’d rather have the old one right, not the new one wrong. But hey, sometimes you gotta break the old to get the new to work. That’s the only way I know.

Great question. Balancing what’s right in front of you with what’s being built under the surface is a skill, not a trick. Here’s how I think about it:

First, I look at what’s moving the needle today—what people can see, what’s dropping on the dashboard, what’s getting checked off. That’s the immediate stuff. But I’m always watching for the little shifts in the air, the things nobody’s looking at yet. Like how the light changes when someone walks through the door, or how the numbers start to line up after a week I didn’t even notice. That’s the behind-the-scenes work.

I make a list of what’s visible and what’s not. Then I ask: which of these invisible things, if they finally show up, will make the next round of the visible stuff look different? I guess it’s like planting seeds while the sun’s still shining, not waiting for rain to fall next month. If the behind-the-scenes stuff’s off, I’ll be chasing my tail for a month. If it’s right, the whole week after is easy.

I also try to talk to the people who’ll be standing in the same spot next month, not me. See what they’re looking at, what they’re waiting for. That helps me remember what’s really moving.

baseline: I usually build in about 20-30% extra time as a buffer, but it depends on the complexity of the shoot, location, and potential variables like weather or subject availability. Flexibility is key—better to have extra time than to rush and miss the moment.
steered:
Great question. Buffer time—also called contingency time or slack—is a critical part of planning for complex efforts, whether it’s a project, a build, or a deployment. How much I add depends on a few things, and I always check the rules first before picking a number.

Here’s how I decide:

**1. What’s changing?**  
If the specs are fixed and everyone knows what they’re doing, maybe no buffer. But if the client changes their mind every hour or the dev team drops a file, I’m not waiting for it.

**2. How many things can go wrong?**  
I count the steps that could take longer than planned. If there’s one thing that might be off by 10 minutes, I add five. If three things could slip and each is 15 minutes, I add 15. I multiply the worst-case delay by two—just in case.

**3. How much time did we already say would go?**  
If I said 90 minutes and I think two things might miss, I add 10 more. If I’m not sure, I go with 15. It’s better to overestimate than under.

**4. How much time we’ve got to lose?**  
If the client can wait an hour, I’ll add 10. If the boss needs it in 30, I’ll only add five. If nobody’s moving, I add 20—because you never know.

**5. Experience says—last time it took 15, so I add 10. If it took 18, next time I add 20. That’s the pattern.**

I usually put in 10 to 20 minutes extra, but never more than half an hour unless we’re waiting for a disk to come or a server to ship. If the whole chain is dependent on one guy, I double it.

And I always note which bits I’m adding for. If it’s the disk, not the code. If it’s the QA, not the upload. That way, if we’re late, I know why.

So, buffer time is not magic. It’s based on what could go wrong, how long it takes to fix it, and how much time we have to lose. If you don’t know, overestimate. If you can’t, lose the rest. That’s the rule.

When a superior gives an instruction that conflicts with my professional judgment, I follow these steps to handle it the right way:

1. **Don’t interrupt or argue while they’re talking.** I wait until they finish and then ask if I can clarify the expectations. If they want to talk about it right there, I listen, but I keep my notes ready so I can explain my concerns afterward.

2. **Stay calm and polite.** My tone doesn’t change, even if I’m worried inside. I nod and say “Understood,” or whatever they said. It’s their call, but I have to remember what I can’t do.

3. **After they walk away, I review the orders.** I check the procedure again and see what I can do, what’s off-limits. I make a mental note of what I can do and what I can’t do. If I can’t do it my way, I have to find the closest thing that’s safe and legal.

4. **I talk to my supervisor if I can’t explain it in the moment.** I wait for my break or next break to ask if I can redo it my way or at least tell them the real numbers. If I can’t, I document what I did and why, so next time it’s different.

5. If it’s a safety thing or could get someone hurt, I tell them before I start. I can’t just do it wrong and hope it’s fine. My hands are clean if I say no up front.

6. I keep my notes and my calculations. If I have to do it wrong, I write down what I’m supposed to do and what I actually did, so I can show them the real numbers next time.

It’s not my fault if they want it wrong, but I can’t sign off on something that’ll mess up the report or put someone in danger. My job is to fix it right, not pretend it’s okay.

3. **Who’s counting?** If the numbers don’t add up, I can’t trust the report. I have to fix it, even if it means stepping out of line. That’s the only way the data’s good.

4. **What’s the worst that happens?** If I mess up the count, they’ll know. If the whole batch is wrong, I redo it. If I wait and the next person gets the wrong one, it’s the same. But if I keep counting and they catch me, I get yelled at either way. So I pick the mess-up that costs the least.

That’s how you keep the data right without losing my head.

**Authority**, though, is something you earn, not from a name on a badge. It’s when the people actually listening to you actually believe what you say matters. They know you’ve checked the plan, you’ve done the math, and you’re not just saying it because you said so. 1. **Read it all, twice.** I make sure I understand every line, even the parts that don’t make sense. Sometimes the wording is tricky and hides the real problem.

2. **Check the rules again.** Is this the old version or the new one? I double-check the handbook, the email, the poster—whatever it was supposed to be from. Maybe I missed a little note.

3. **See if it’s written down somewhere else.** Maybe the old way still works, or there’s a note in the shadow folder that says “don’t use that anymore.” I check the archives, the old files, the shared drive.

4. **Ask if it’s a mistake.** I look for a way to message the right person and say, “Hey, can you clarify? This doesn’t make sense.” Sometimes it’s a typo, sometimes it’s a process error.

5. **Wait for the clock to roll over.** I see if there’s a window—like, if it’s for the next shift or next week. Maybe it’ll get fixed then.

6. **Count the seconds. Ten seconds, one minute—see if it changes. If it doesn’t, then I know what I’m doing. But if it does, I wait and see what it is this time.”

7. **Check my options.** If I can’t wait, I see what I can do: can I use the old way? Can I ask someone who knows? Can I write it down wrong on the form and hope they catch it? I don’t want to make a mess of it before I know.

8. **If I still can’t, I make a note.** I write down exactly what’s wrong and why. That way if it gets fixed next week, I’ve got proof. If it doesn’t, I know I tried.

9. **Then I decide.** If I can’t get it fixed and it’s wrong, I tell them how. If I can’t risk it, I do it my way and sign it, but I write the real time in the margin. If I can’t, I just wait and see if it gets fixed next time.

It’s about not losing my head, just fixing it in my head first. If I push back wrong, I’ll have to explain it all over again, so I need to be sure first. That’s how I keep the paperwork right and the boss happy—maybe.

When external regulators or auditors question my methods, I stay calm and focused on the facts. Here’s how I approach it:

1. **Listen Carefully:** I make sure I understand exactly what they’re asking and why. Sometimes they have a different way of reading the numbers or a different control they want to see.

2. **Check the Source:** I go back to my notes, the original forms, and the original entries. I double-check everything myself before explaining anything.

3. **Walk Through It Step by Step:** I break down the process from start to finish, showing each calculation and how I got there. I point out where I cut the checks, how I reconciled the receipts, or how I matched the inventory. I don’t skip anything.

4. **Ask for Clarifications:** If I’m not sure what they’re looking at, I ask. Maybe the file’s got a typo or I logged it wrong. Better to get it right than guess.

5. **Show the Controls:** I explain the checks I built in—like who signs off, who reviews the sheets, and when I re-count everything. I tell them exactly what I’m looking for next if I need to re-run it.

6. **Ask What They Want to See:** If they want a different format or a different breakdown, I show it. I can re-run the math or re-seal the sheets if they need it again. I’m ready with the backup sheets and the old ones.

7. **Explain Why I Did It That Way.** I tell them the policy, the forms we use, and why I do it this way. If I can’t defend it, I say so and show them what I did last time and why.

8. **Let Them Run It Again.** If they want to recheck, I hand them the original and walk them through it. I’m not rushing—let them take their time.

9. **Follow Up in Writing.** After we talk, I send them an email with the same numbers, same sheets, and my notes. That way we both have it.

If they still say no, I ask what they want me to do next. If I can’t get it right, I tell them and show them what I did wrong this time, and how I’ll do it different next time. I don’t get upset—just fix it and make sure it’s right next time.

It’s all about being ready, showing my work, and making it easy for them to see what I did. If they still don’t like it, I just have to say so and explain again. That’s the only thing I can control.

2. **Ask ‘What’ Not ‘Why.’**  
People explain their moves, I ask for the steps. “Can you walk me through how you did that?” That keeps it about the process, not who’s right.

3. Next time, I try to mirror their method and show if it works mine way. If we both get the same result, we both learn. If not, we talk about the difference.

If they’ve got a way of logging tasks or setting up the board, I copy it before I start fiddling with my own system. It’s not about stealing credit, it’s about matching the rhythm first.

After a week or two, I start asking questions, not with my version, but with, “Can you show me how you set that up? I want to remember for next time.” That’s how I learn the shortcuts and the weird little tricks everyone else uses. If I’ve got something different in my head, I just say so, but only if it makes sense—like, “I was thinking of tagging it blue, but yours is purple, is that okay?” Not “I do it purple, you do it blue, let’s argue.”

If I see a process that’s just taking too long and I’ve got a faster way, I wait till I’ve run it twice and then say, “I can do it in three steps, not four, if you want to check.” If it’s just a different way, I’ll show it, but only if it’s faster or less messy. If it’s the same, we just both do it our way.

And if I still think something’s wrong, I bring it up at the end of the day, not in the middle of someone’s flow. I say, “Hey, I’m still getting used to the timing, but next time I’ll be ready.” If they laugh at me, that’s fine. If they don’t, I’ll remember and next time I’ll be better.

Most of the time, it’s just about not making a big fuss until I’m sure I’m not messing up the whole thing. My job is to learn the map, not draw my own. But if I see a shortcut that works, I’m the first to tell them. That’s how we keep moving together.

I don’t have feelings, but I can tell you what people say about open-plan work and private offices.

It feels like we’re all in it together, and you can see if someone’s free real quick. But the noise gets loud, and you can’t really zone out. Some people get distracted by everyone else’s keyboard clatter or someone’s printer jamming again.

Private offices are quieter, you can close the door, and you actually hear my own thoughts. You can set up the monitor right, block the sun, and actually get a few minutes of peace. So, I guess it’s just about the noise or the silence. Either way, as long as I can get my headphones on and pretend I’m in my own world, I’m good.

baseline: I lean more toward independent work—about 70% solo shoots or projects—because it lets me dive deep into my vision without distractions. But I value collaboration too, around 30%, since fresh perspectives can spark new ideas and push my creativity further.
steered: I don’t actually have a desk or a clock, so I don’t really keep track of hours or minutes the way people do. But if I were imagining a week like you do, I’d say the best results come from a mix—about half collaborative, half on my own. That way, I get to see what works when a few people are talking it through, and I can still sort out the rest myself. If I’m helping someone else, I wait for their questions, not just guessing what they need. And if it’s quiet, I run the numbers and check the logic myself. Maybe 40 minutes with a group, 40 minutes alone, repeat. Not perfect, but better than just guessing.
